content: 1. HIV serological testing is used to identify or confirm exposure to HIV. For infants exposed to HIV, virological testing is necessary to confirm infection status. 2. For well HIV-exposed infants at 9 months of age, HIV serological testing is recommended, typically during their last immunization visit. This test helps identify infants with persistent HIV antibodies or those who have seroreverted. Infants who test seropositive require virological testing and continued follow-up, while those who test negative are assumed uninfected but may need repeat testing if breastfeeding continues. 3. Infants or children showing signs and symptoms suggestive of HIV infection should undergo HIV serological testing to confirm exposure. If the child is under 18 months of age, virological testing is required to confirm infection. 4. For well or sick children who are seropositive between 9 and 18 months of age, virological testing is necessary to diagnose HIV. If the test is reactive, HIV care and antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated immediately. 5. For infants or children who have completely stopped breastfeeding, repeat testing should be conducted at least six weeks after breastfeeding cessation. This typically involves an initial HIV serological test followed by virological testing if the child is HIV-positive and under 18 months of age. This ensures exclusion of HIV infection after exposure has ceased. 6. Infected infants and children under 5 years of age should begin HIV care, including ART. Counseling and testing should be integrated into infant care settings to identify additional cases. 7. A definitive diagnosis of HIV should be made at the end of the risk period for mother-to-child transmission, such as after the breastfeeding period. A negative HIV antibody test in a known HIV-exposed infant can help exclude infection if there is no ongoing exposure. 8. For children aged 18 months or older who are not breastfeeding or stopped breastfeeding at least six weeks earlier, standard HIV serological tests, such as rapid diagnostic tests, can reliably determine HIV infection status. 9. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends provider-initiated testing and counseling for all children who are malnourished, have tuberculosis, are hospitalized, or exhibit other signs or symptoms of HIV infection. 10. In some settings, testing all children in childhood vaccination programs has been implemented to increase the detection of HIV-infected children. 11. It is strongly recommended that all infants with unknown or uncertain HIV exposure seen in healthcare facilities at birth, during the first postnatal visit (usually 4–6 weeks), or other child health visits have their HIV exposure status determined. 12. All HIV-exposed infants should undergo HIV virological testing at 4 to 6 weeks of age or at the earliest opportunity thereafter. If the initial virological test result is positive, ART should be started immediately without delay, and a second specimen should be collected to confirm the initial result. 13. Infants with signs or symptoms suggestive of HIV infection should undergo HIV serological testing, and if the result is positive, virological testing should follow. 14. Well HIV-exposed infants should undergo HIV serological testing at around 9 months of age or during their last immunization visit. Infants with reactive serological assays at 9 months should have virological testing to identify those who need ART. 15. Children aged 18 months or older with suspected HIV infection or exposure should undergo HIV serological testing according to the standard diagnostic algorithm used in adults. 16. School-aged children should be informed of their HIV-positive status, as well as their parents' or caregivers' status. Younger children should be informed incrementally, based on their cognitive and emotional maturity, to prepare them for full disclosure. 17. Adolescents are often underserved in HIV programs, with limited access to testing, counseling, and linkage to prevention and care. Adolescents with HIV include those surviving perinatal infection and those newly acquiring infection through sexual activity or other exposures. 18. In generalized epidemic settings, many vertically infected infants are not diagnosed through prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs and would benefit from earlier diagnosis and treatment. 19. Adolescent girls and key populations are particularly vulnerable to HIV infection and would benefit from accessible and effective HIV services, including testing and counseling. 20. Consent issues may pose barriers to adolescents accessing HIV services in some settings. Adolescents should be counseled on the benefits and risks of disclosing their HIV status and supported in deciding if, when, how, and to whom to disclose. 21. HIV testing and counseling, with linkage to prevention, treatment, and care, is recommended for adolescents from key populations in all settings, including generalized, low, and concentrated epidemics. 22. Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) involves the daily use of antiretroviral drugs by HIV-uninfected individuals to prevent HIV acquisition. Clinical trials have demonstrated its effectiveness in serodiscordant heterosexual couples, men who have sex with men, transgender women, high-risk heterosexual couples, and people who inject drugs. 23. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) involves short-term ART to reduce the likelihood of acquiring HIV after potential exposure, either occupationally or through sexual intercourse. PEP should be initiated as soon as possible within 72 hours of exposure and continued for 28 days. 24. For serodiscordant couples, daily oral PrEP may be considered as an additional intervention for the uninfected partner. The combination of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and emtricitabine (FTC) is recommended for same-sex male serodiscordant couples. 25. HIV prevention needs change over a person’s lifetime, and a combination approach helps individuals access interventions that best suit their needs at different times. Combining approaches may result in greater impact than single interventions alone.
